stanzas: தோடு டையசெவி யன்விடை யேறியோர் தூவெண் மதிசூடிக்
காடு டையசுட லைப்பொடி பூசியென் னுள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
ஏடு டையமல ரான்முனை நாட்பணிந் தேத்த வருள் செய்த
பீடு டைய பிரமாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
முற்ற லாமையிள நாகமோ டேன முளைக் கொம் பவைபூண்டு
வற்ற லோடுகல னாப்பலி தேர்ந்தென துள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
கற்றல் கேட்டலுடை யார்பெரி யார்கழல் கையாற் றொழுதேத்தப்
பெற்ற மூர்ந்தபிர மாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
நீர்ப ரந்தநிமிர் புன்சடை மேலோர் நிலாவெண் மதிசூடி
ஏர்ப ரந்தவின வெள்வளை சோரவென் னுள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
ஊர்ப ரந்தவுல கின்முத லாகிய வோரூ ரிதுவென்னப்
பேர்ப ரந்தபிர மாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
விண்ம கிழ்ந்தமதி லெய்தது மன்றிவி ளங்கு தலையோட்டில்
உண்ம கிழ்ந்துபலி தேரிய வந்தென துள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
மண்ம கிழ்ந்தவர வம்மலர்க் கொன்றை மலிந்த வரைமார்பில்
பெண்ம கிழ்ந்தபிர மாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
ஒருமை பெண்மையுடை யன்சடை யன்விடை யூரும் மிவனென்ன
அருமை யாகவுரை செய்ய வமர்ந்தென துள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
கருமை பெற்றகடல் கொள்ளமி தந்ததோர் காலம் மிதுவென்னப்
பெருமை பெற்றபிர மாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
மறைக லந்தவொலி பாடலோ டாடல ராகி மழுவேந்தி
இறைக லந்தவின வெள்வளை சோரவென் னுள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
கறைக லந்தகடி யார்பொழி னீடுயர் சோலைக் கதிர்சிந்தப்
பிறைக லந்த பிரமாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
சடைமு யங்குபுன லன்னன லன்னெரி வீசிச் சதிர்வெய்த
உடைமு யங்குமர வோடுழி தந்தென துள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
கடன்மு யங்குகழி சூழ்குளிர் கானலம் பொன்னஞ் சிறகன்னம்
பெடைமு யங்குபிர மாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
வியரி லங்குவரை யுந்திய தோள்களை வீரம் விளைவித்த
உயரி லங்கையரை யன்வலி செற்றென துள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
துயரி லங்குமுல கிற்பல வூழிக டோன்றும் பொழுதெல்லாம்
பெயரி லங்குபிர மாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
தாணு தல்செய்திறை காணிய மாலொடு தண்டா மரையானும்
நீணு தல்செய்தொழி யந்நிமிர்ந் தானென துள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
வாணு தல்செய்மக ளீர்முத லாகிய வையத் தவரேத்தப்
பேணு தல்செய்பிர மாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
புத்த ரோடுபொறி யில்சமணும்புறங் கூற நெறிநில்லா
ஒத்த சொல்லவுல கம்பலி தேர்ந்தென துள்ளங் கவர்கள்வன்
மத்த யானைமறு கவ்வுரி போர்த்ததோர் மாயம் மிதுவென்னப்
பித்தர் போலும்பிர மாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவனன்றே
அருநெ றியமறை வல்ல முனியகன் பொய்கை யலர்மேய
பெருநெ றியபிர மாபுர மேவிய பெம்மா னிவன்றன்னை
ஒருநெ றியமனம் வைத்துணர் ஞானசம் பந்தன் னுரை செய்த
திருநெ றியதமிழ் வல்லவர் தொல்வினை தீர்த லெளிதாமே

stanzas: He of the ear that bears the earring, who has mounted the bull, wearing a pure white moon,
smeared with the ash of the cremation ground of the wilds, the thief who stole my heart,
who gave his grace when, in a day of old, he of the petalled flower bowed down and praised him:
the Lord who dwells in glorious Piramāpuram, is it not he?
Wearing an old tortoise's shell, a young snake and the young tusk of a boar,
seeking alms with a dried skull for his bowl, the thief who stole my heart,
while the great ones, rich in learning and in listening, worship his anklets with their hands and praise him:
the Lord who rides the bull and dwells in Piramāpuram, is it not he?
Wearing a white moon of moonlight on his upright, tawny matted locks where the water spreads,
so that my row of lovely white bangles slips away, the thief who stole my heart,
so that men say, 'This is the one town that was first in the world where towns spread wide':
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, whose name has spread, is it not he?
Not only did he shoot the walled cities that rejoiced in the sky; with a gleaming skull-bowl
he came, glad at heart, seeking alms, the thief who stole my heart;
on his mountain-like chest, rich with the earth-loving snake and koṉṟai flowers,
the Lord who rejoices in the woman and dwells in Piramāpuram, is it not he?
'He has oneness and womanhood, he has matted locks, it is he who rides the bull,' so they say,
and as they speak of him as hard to reach, he settled here, the thief who stole my heart;
so that men say, 'This floated in that one age when the dark sea seized all':
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, which won greatness, is it not he?
Becoming a dancer to songs whose sound is mingled with the Vedas, holding the battle-axe,
so that the row of white bangles on my wrist slips away, the thief who stole my heart;
where the tall, lofty groves, dark and full of fragrance, scatter the rays [?],
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, where the crescent moon mingles, is it not he?
He with the river clasped in his matted locks, he of the fire, swinging the flame, winning splendour [?],
wandering with the snake that clasps his garment, the thief who stole my heart;
in the cool seashore groves ringed by backwaters that clasp the sea, the lovely golden-winged swan
clasps its mate in Piramāpuram: the Lord who dwells there, is it not he?
The shoulders that, glistening with sweat [?], heaved up the mountain, that bred such valour:
he crushed the strength of the king of lofty Laṅkā, the thief who stole my heart;
in this world where sorrow shows itself, whenever the many ages appear,
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, whose name shines, is it not he?
As Māl and he of the cool lotus strove to see the feet and the brow of the Lord,
he stretched out and rose so high that they gave up, the thief who stole my heart;
while the people of the world, the women of bright brow first among them, praise him,
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, which cherishes him, is it not he?
While the Buddhists and the witless Jains speak ill of him behind his back, keeping to no true path,
and speak alike [?], he sought alms through the world, the thief who stole my heart;
so that men say, 'This is a marvel, that he wrapped himself in the hide of the rutting elephant as it reeled':
the Lord who dwells in Piramāpuram, like one who is mad, is it not he?
The sage, master of the Vedas of the hard path, who dwells on the flower of the wide pool—
his Piramāpuram of the great path, and the Lord who dwells there: of him
Ñāṉacampantaṉ, who knows him with a mind set on the one path, has spoken
this Tamil of the holy path; for those who know it well, to be rid of their old deeds becomes easy.

notes: Romanized as written, including the metrical splits of the printed text, which cut words at the feet of the verse ('tōṭu ṭaiyacevi yaṉviṭai' for tōṭuṭaiya ceviyaṉ viṭai; 'pemmā ṉivaṉaṉṟē' for pemmāṉ ivaṉ aṉṟē), as in the site's Tiruppavai. ISO 15919 for Tamil: letters as written (k, c, ṭ, t, p whatever their sound), ṉ ன, ṟ ற, ḻ ழ, ḷ ள, e/ē and o/ō kept apart.

Last line of every stanza: 'pemmāṉ ivaṉ aṉṟē', 'is not this one the Lord (pemmāṉ, the great lord)?', rendered 'the Lord who dwells in … Piramāpuram, is it not he?'. Second line of stanzas 1-10: 'eṉ uḷḷam kavar kaḷvaṉ', 'the thief who stole my heart'.

Piramāpuram (Brahmapuram, 'the city of Brahmā') is a name of the town Cīrkāḻi (Sirkazhi). Each stanza's last line gives the town or the Lord an epithet: glorious, whose name has spread, which won greatness, whose name shines, which cherishes him.
The singer speaks as a woman in love: her bangles slipping from her wrist (3.2, 6.2) is the conventional sign, in Tamil love poetry, of a woman wasting with longing.

line 1.1: tōṭu is an ear-ornament (a rolled leaf or ring) worn by women; it is usually taken to show that half of the god's body is the goddess. 'tū veṇ mati', 'pure white moon', is the crescent he wears.
line 1.3: 'ēṭuṭaiya malarāṉ', 'he of the flower with petals', is Brahmā, seated on the lotus; so also 9.1 ('he of the cool lotus') and 11.1 ('who dwells on the flower of the wide pool').
line 2.1: 'muṟṟal āmai', a full-grown (old) tortoise, its shell worn as an ornament; 'ēṉam muḷai kompu', the boar's sprouting (young) tusk.
line 2.3: kaḻal is the warrior's anklet, here standing for his feet; 'kaiyāl toḻutu', worshipping with the hands, i.e. with joined palms.
line 3.1: 'puṉ caṭai', matted locks that are puṉ: tawny, reddish, or thin; 'nīr paranta', where water spreads, i.e. the river held in his hair. 'nilā veṇ mati', a white moon of moonlight.
line 3.3 and 5.3: the town is praised as the first of all towns and as the one that floated when the dark sea covered everything (mitantatu, 'floated').
line 4.1: 'viṇ makiḻnta matil', 'walls that rejoiced in the sky': the flying fortified cities the god destroyed with an arrow (eytatu, 'shot').
line 4.2: 'uḷ makiḻntu' (written uṇmakiḻntu), 'glad at heart'.
line 4.3: koṉṟai, the Indian laburnum (Cassia fistula), whose golden flowers the god wears; 'maṇ makiḻnta aravam', the snake that delights in the earth.
line 4.4: 'peṇ makiḻnta', 'who rejoices in the woman': the goddess, joined to him; it could also be read as describing the town.
line 5.1: 'orumai peṇmai uṭaiyaṉ', 'he who has oneness and womanhood': usually read as one being who is also woman (the form half male, half female); the construction is disputed.
line 5.2: 'arumai āka urai ceyya amarntu': 'as they speak of him as rare (hard to attain), he settled (here)'; amarntu can also be 'gladly abiding'.
line 6.1: 'maṟai kalanta oli pāṭalōṭu āṭalar āki', 'becoming a dancer, with songs whose sound is mixed with the Vedas'; maḻu, the battle-axe.
line 6.3: 'kaṟai kalanta', 'mixed with darkness' (deep shade); 'katir cinta', 'so that the rays scatter': whose rays (the sun's, the moon's) and how the groves scatter them is not clear [?].
line 6.4: 'piṟai kalanta', 'with which the crescent moon mingles': either the town, whose groves reach the crescent, or the Lord, who wears it.
line 7.1: 'catir eyta' (written catirveyta): catir is excellence, splendour or grace in the dance; the sense of the phrase is uncertain [?]. 'eri vīci', swinging or flinging fire.

Wordplay: each stanza repeats one word or sound at the head of all four lines: uṭaiya 'having' (1), -ṟṟa (2), paranta 'spread' (3), makiḻnta 'rejoicing' (4), -rumai (5), kalanta 'mingled' (6), muyaṅku 'clasp, embrace' (7), ilaṅku 'shine, show' (8), -ṇutal cey (9), -tta (10), neṟi 'path' (11). The translation keeps the repeated English word where it can ('clasp' in 7).

line 8.1-8.2: the king of lofty Laṅkā (Rāvaṇa) lifting the mountain; viyar is read as 'sweat' [?] (also possible: 'great, wide'). 'vīram viḷaivitta', 'which produced valour': it may describe the shoulders or the king.
line 8.3: ūḻi, an aeon, a world-age.
line 9.1: 'tāṇutal' is tāḷ 'foot' + nutal 'brow': Māl (Viṣṇu) and Brahmā seeking the feet and the head of the god, who (9.2) grew beyond them until they gave up (oḻiya).
line 9.3: 'vāḷ nutal makaḷir', 'women of shining brow'. 9.4 'pēṇutal cey', 'which cherishes, worships': the town (or the Lord who cherishes it).
line 10.1: camaṇ, the Jains (Śramaṇas); 'poṟi il', 'without sense' or 'luckless'. 'puṟaṅ kūṟa', 'speak behind his back, slander'.
line 10.1-10.2: 'neṟi nillā otta colla' is hard to construe [?]: 'those who keep to no path speaking alike (with one voice)', or 'speaking words that agree (with the world)'.
line 10.3: 'matta yāṉai', the rutting or maddened elephant; maṟuka, 'so that it was bewildered, reeled'; uri, its hide; māyam, a marvel or illusion.
line 10.4: 'pittar pōlum', 'like one mad': Pittaṉ, 'the mad one', is an epithet of the god; pōlum may also be a softening particle ('it seems').
line 11.3: Ñāṉacampantaṉ (Jñānasambandar, Sambandar) names himself, as the closing stanza of a patikam does; 'oru neṟiya maṉam vaittu uṇar', 'who knows (him) having set his mind on the single path'.
line 11.4: tolviṉai, 'old deeds': the karma of former births; 'tīrtal eḷitu ām', 'ending them becomes easy'. 'Tamil' is the song itself.
